gloss: The sugar found in sugarcane and beets, the kind sold as ordinary table sugar.
examples: Table sugar is almost pure *sucrose*.
The label lists *sucrose* as the second ingredient.
Fruit contains fructose as well as *sucrose*.

gloss: The force that pulls air, liquid, or an object toward a space where the pressure is lower.
examples: The vacuum has lost most of its *suction*.
The dentist used *suction* to keep my mouth dry.
The hook stays on the tile by *suction*.

gloss: A number puzzle in which you fill a grid so that no digit repeats in a row, column, or box.
examples: She does a *sudoku* with her morning coffee.
The back page has a crossword and two *sudokus*.
This *sudoku* is rated hard.

gloss: Death or distress caused by not being able to breathe.
examples: The medical examiner gave the cause of death as *suffocation*.
The warning says the plastic bag is a *suffocation* hazard.
In house fires, smoke and *suffocation* kill more people than flames do.

gloss: A woman who campaigned for women's right to vote in the early twentieth century.
examples: Her great-grandmother was a *suffragette*.
The museum has photographs of *suffragettes* marching in London.
The film follows a young *suffragette* through her first arrest.
contrast: American writing usually says *suffragist* for the U.S. movement; *suffragette* refers mainly to the British campaigners.

gloss: Someone who campaigned for the right to vote, especially for women.
examples: American *suffragists* won the vote in 1920.
She wrote a biography of a Tennessee *suffragist*.
The parade honored the *suffragists* of a century ago.

gloss: The tall tropical grass whose stems are crushed to make sugar.
examples: The island's economy once depended entirely on *sugarcane*.
They sell fresh *sugarcane* juice at the market.
Fields of *sugarcane* stretched to the horizon.

gloss: An idea that you put forward for someone to consider.
examples: Can I make a *suggestion*?
Her *suggestion* saved us two days of work.
The box by the door is for comments and *suggestions*.

gloss: How well something or someone fits a particular purpose.
examples: The committee questioned his *suitability* for the job.
Test the soil for *suitability* before you plant.
Each site was rated for *suitability* and cost.

ru: поклонник, ухажёр; претендент на покупку компании
gloss: A man hoping to marry a particular woman, or a company hoping to buy another one.
examples: In the novel she turns away every *suitor*.
The startup attracted three *suitors* before the sale.
Her parents approved of the new *suitor*.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A salt of sulfuric acid, found in fertilizers, detergents, and shampoos.
examples: This shampoo is free of *sulfates*.
The fertilizer contains ammonium *sulfate*.
High *sulfate* levels made the well water taste odd.
contrast: American spelling is *sulfate*; British writing uses *sulphate*.

gloss: A Muslim ruler, especially of one of the older Middle Eastern or North African states.
examples: The *sultan* built the mosque in the sixteenth century.
Oman is still ruled by a *sultan*.
Three *sultans* lived in this palace.

gloss: A shrub with clusters of dark red berries, one American kind of which causes a rash.
examples: Watch out for poison *sumac* along the trail.
The *sumac* by the driveway turns bright red in October.
Middle Eastern cooks sprinkle ground *sumac* over salads.
contrast: Both SOO-mak and SHOO-mak are heard in American English.

gloss: The Japanese style of wrestling in which two heavy fighters try to push each other out of a ring.
examples: He watches *sumo* on TV every January.
*Sumo* has strict rules about ceremony and dress.
They went to a *sumo* tournament in Tokyo.

gloss: A ray of sunlight, especially one you can see coming through an opening.
examples: A *sunbeam* fell across the kitchen table.
The cat sleeps in the *sunbeam* by the window.
*Sunbeams* came through the gaps in the barn roof.

gloss: A light sleeveless dress for hot weather.
examples: She wore a yellow *sundress* to the picnic.
I packed two *sundresses* and a pair of sandals.
That *sundress* is too thin for a windy day.

gloss: A dark, cooler patch on the surface of the sun.
examples: *Sunspots* follow a cycle of about eleven years.
A large *sunspot* was visible through the filter.
The radio blackout came from a flare near a *sunspot*.

gloss: A germ that has become resistant to most antibiotics.
examples: The hospital is fighting a *superbug* that resists most drugs.
Overusing antibiotics helps create *superbugs*.
The outbreak was traced to a *superbug* in the intensive care unit.

gloss: A device driven by an engine that forces extra air into it for more power.
examples: The car has a *supercharger* instead of a turbo.
He rebuilt the *supercharger* over the winter.
*Superchargers* deliver power right away at low speeds.

gloss: The state of being better, stronger, or higher in rank than someone else.
examples: He talks to everyone with an air of *superiority*.
The team's *superiority* was obvious by halftime.
Air *superiority* decided the outcome of the battle.

gloss: A very famous, highly paid fashion model.
examples: She became a *supermodel* at nineteen.
The show closed with three *supermodels* on the runway.
The magazine put a *supermodel* on the cover again.

gloss: The enormous explosion of a dying star.
examples: A *supernova* can briefly outshine an entire galaxy.
Astronomers spotted two *supernovas* in the same month.
The heavy elements in our bodies came from a *supernova*.
contrast: Ordinary American writing uses the plural *supernovas*; astronomers often write *supernovae*.

gloss: A small character printed above the line, like the 2 in x squared.
examples: The footnote number appears as a *superscript*.
Type the exponent as a *superscript*.
The program turns those digits into *superscripts* automatically.

gloss: The act of watching over people or work to make sure it is done properly.
examples: Children need adult *supervision* at the pool.
He works under the *supervision* of a licensed engineer.
The lab has almost no *supervision* on weekends.

gloss: Someone who backs a person, team, or cause.
examples: She thanked her *supporters* after the vote.
He has been a *supporter* of the local team since childhood.
The bill has *supporters* in both parties.

gloss: An idea taken to be true without proof.
examples: The whole plan rests on one *supposition*.
That is a reasonable *supposition*, but we need evidence.
His argument is built on *suppositions*, not facts.

gloss: A small piece of medicine shaped to be inserted into the body, where it melts.
examples: The pharmacist recommended a *suppository* for the fever.
*Suppositories* help when a child cannot keep pills down.
Store the *suppositories* in the refrigerator.

gloss: A drug that holds back an unwanted body reaction such as coughing or hunger.
examples: The syrup contains a cough *suppressant*.
Appetite *suppressants* are sold all over the internet.
The doctor prescribed a *suppressant* for the tremors.

gloss: The act of stopping something by force, or of keeping it from being known.
examples: The report described the *suppression* of the protests.
Voter *suppression* was the central issue in the lawsuit.
The warehouse has an automatic fire *suppression* system.

ru: сторонник превосходства своей расы или группы
gloss: Someone who believes that one race or group should rule over the others.
examples: The rally drew a few dozen white *supremacists*.
He denies ever having been a *supremacist*.
The forum shut down after *supremacists* took it over.

gloss: An art movement that combines dreamlike, impossible images.
examples: The exhibit traces *surrealism* from Paris to New York.
There is a touch of *surrealism* in her photographs.
He wrote his thesis on *surrealism*.

gloss: A person or thing that takes the place of another.
examples: The couple found a *surrogate* to carry the baby.
For a lot of those kids, the coach became a father *surrogate*.
Sales figures are used as a *surrogate* for demand.

gloss: Someone whose job is to measure and record the boundaries and features of land.
examples: A *surveyor* marked the property line last week.
*Surveyors* found that the fence sits two feet over.
You will need a licensed *surveyor* before you build.

gloss: Food and drink that keeps a person or animal alive.
examples: The refugees had little *sustenance* for the journey.
Bread and beans were their only *sustenance* that winter.
The plant draws *sustenance* from the thin soil.

gloss: A stitch used by a surgeon to close a wound.
examples: The nurse removed the *sutures* after ten days.
He needed four *sutures* above his eyebrow.
The *suture* held even after the swelling went down.

gloss: A small piece of soft material on a stick, used to clean a wound or collect a sample.
examples: The nurse took a throat *swab*.
Clean the cut with an alcohol *swab*.
They shipped the *swabs* to the lab the same day.

gloss: Free promotional items handed out at an event or by a company.
examples: The conference *swag* included a T-shirt and a water bottle.
She came home with a whole bag of *swag*.
Everyone who registers gets some *swag* at the door.

gloss: A cross with bent arms, an ancient symbol later used by the Nazis.
examples: Someone painted a *swastika* on the synagogue wall.
The flag carried a black *swastika* in a white circle.
Police are investigating the *swastikas* found on campus.

gloss: A long, broad strip of land or of anything spread out.
examples: The fire burned a *swath* through the forest.
Large *swaths* of the state lost power.
He cut a neat *swath* across the lawn with the mower.
contrast: Americans say SWAHTH and spell it *swath*; the spelling *swathe* is mainly British.

gloss: A flat tool on a handle used for killing flies.
examples: Grab the fly *swatter* — there is a wasp in the kitchen.
He keeps a *swatter* hanging by the back door.
The kids argued over who got the *swatter*.

gloss: A contest in which the winners are drawn at random for prizes.
examples: She entered a *sweepstakes* to win a car.
The magazine runs a *sweepstakes* every summer.
No purchase is necessary to enter the *sweepstakes*.
contrast: The word keeps its -s even in the singular: *a sweepstakes*, not a sweepstake.

gloss: A person you love romantically, or a warm way of addressing someone.
examples: They were high school *sweethearts*.
Thanks for waiting, *sweetheart*.
He sent his *sweetheart* flowers on her birthday.

gloss: The quality of tasting like sugar, or of being gentle and kind.
examples: The sauce needs a little *sweetness* to balance the vinegar.
There is a *sweetness* in the way he talks about his grandmother.
Fresh corn has a natural *sweetness* that fades in a day.

gloss: Someone who cheats people out of their money.
examples: The *swindler* took her entire life savings.
Police arrested two *swindlers* running a fake charity.
He turned out to be a *swindler*, not an investor.

ru: движение пальцем по экрану; удар вскользь; выпад
gloss: A quick sliding movement of the finger across a screen, or a sweeping blow or pointed remark.
examples: Unlock the phone with a *swipe*.
The bear took a *swipe* at the cooler.
The senator took a *swipe* at her opponent in the first minute.

gloss: A pocket knife whose blade springs out when you press a button.
examples: *Switchblades* are illegal in several states.
He pulled a *switchblade* out of his jacket.
The prop was a rubber *switchblade* that could not cut anything.

gloss: The central panel through which telephone calls in an organization are connected.
examples: Call the hospital *switchboard* and ask for the front desk.
The *switchboard* lit up right after the announcement.
She worked a hotel *switchboard* in the 1960s.

gloss: A large shade tree with pale flaking bark, common along American rivers and streets.
examples: A huge *sycamore* shades the whole backyard.
The street is lined with *sycamores*.
The old *sycamore* lost a limb in the storm.
contrast: The American *sycamore* is a plane tree; in Britain the same word names a kind of maple.

gloss: Someone who flatters powerful people in order to gain something.
examples: The boss is surrounded by *sycophants*.
Nobody wants to be seen as a *sycophant*.
The column called him a *sycophant* with no ideas of his own.

gloss: A mark, sign, or object that stands for something else.
examples: The dove is a *symbol* of peace.
What does this *symbol* on the map mean?
Chemical *symbols* are listed in the front of the book.
contrast: Sounds exactly like *cymbal*, the metal disc in a drum set.

gloss: The use of symbols to suggest deeper meanings, especially in art and writing.
examples: The essay discusses the *symbolism* of the river in the novel.
There is obvious *symbolism* in choosing that date for the signing.
Students learn to spot *symbolism* in poetry.

gloss: Someone who quietly supports a cause or group without openly joining it.
examples: He was arrested as a *sympathizer* of the rebels.
The party counts on quiet *sympathizers* in the suburbs.
She was accused of being a *sympathizer* and lost her job.

gloss: The tiny gap where one nerve cell passes a signal to the next.
examples: Learning strengthens the *synapses* between neurons.
The drug acts on one particular kind of *synapse*.
Millions of *synapses* form in a baby's first year.

gloss: A rhythm that stresses the offbeats instead of the expected strong beats.
examples: Ragtime is built on *syncopation*.
The drummer added some *syncopation* to the chorus.
*Syncopation* is what gives the tune its swing.

gloss: A group of people or companies working together in business or in crime.
examples: A drug *syndicate* controlled the whole port.
Six banks formed a *syndicate* to finance the deal.
The comic strip runs through a newspaper *syndicate*.
contrast: The noun ends in -kut (SIN-dih-kut); the verb *syndicate* ends in -kayt.

ru: синдикация (продажа прав на показ или публикацию)
gloss: The sale of a show, column, or loan to many outlets or lenders at once.
examples: The sitcom made most of its money in *syndication*.
Reruns went into *syndication* after the fifth season.
The loan was arranged through *syndication* among six banks.

gloss: The extra benefit that comes when two people or groups work together.
examples: There is real *synergy* between the two teams.
The merger was pitched on *synergy* between the product lines.
Without *synergy*, the two departments just duplicate each other's work.

gloss: A serious sexually transmitted disease caused by bacteria.
examples: *Syphilis* can be cured with penicillin if it is caught early.
Cases of *syphilis* have risen sharply in several states.
The clinic tests for *syphilis* and HIV at the same visit.

gloss: The flat upper surface of a table.
examples: The *tabletop* is solid walnut.
Wipe the *tabletop* before you set the plates down.
Years of homework had scratched the *tabletop*.

gloss: A short nail with a broad flat head, used to fasten something to a surface.
examples: She hung the poster with four *tacks*.
A *tack* was stuck in the front tire.
Push the map into the corkboard with a *tack*.

gloss: The skill of saying and doing things without upsetting people.
examples: He handled the complaint with real *tact*.
It takes *tact* to tell someone their work is not good enough.
She has no *tact* whatsoever.
contrast: Do not confuse *tact* (politeness) with *tack* (a small nail, or a course of action).

gloss: A particular action chosen to reach a short-term goal.
examples: Delaying the vote was a smart *tactic*.
Their *tactics* have not changed in years.
The company uses pressure *tactics* on customers who pay late.

gloss: A chewy candy made by boiling sugar and pulling it until it is soft and glossy.
examples: We bought saltwater *taffy* on the boardwalk.
The kids pulled *taffy* at the fall festival.
A piece of *taffy* stuck to his back teeth.

gloss: A thick paste made from ground sesame seeds.
examples: Hummus is chickpeas, lemon, garlic, and *tahini*.
Stir the *tahini* well before you measure it out.
The dressing is just *tahini* thinned with water.

gloss: A steep out-of-control fall, either of an airplane or of something like prices or a mood.
examples: The news sent the stock into a *tailspin*.
The plane went into a *tailspin* over the desert.
After the layoff he went into an emotional *tailspin*.

gloss: A wind blowing from behind, which helps you move faster.
examples: A strong *tailwind* got us to Denver twenty minutes early.
Cyclists love a *tailwind* on the ride home.
Low interest rates were a *tailwind* for the housing market.

gloss: Someone's particular opinion on a subject, or one filmed attempt at a scene.
examples: What is your *take* on the new policy?
The director kept the third *take*.
Her *take* on the book is worth reading.

gloss: The main point you are meant to remember from a talk, meeting, or article.
examples: The big *takeaway* is that costs are rising faster than sales.
Here are three *takeaways* from last night's debate.
My *takeaway* from the class was to start earlier.
contrast: In American English a *takeaway* is a main point; the British also use it for food ordered to go, which Americans call *takeout*.

gloss: A very soft mineral ground into the fine white powder used on skin.
examples: The powder is mostly *talc* and cornstarch.
Some baby powders no longer contain *talc*.
*Talc* is the softest mineral on the hardness scale.
contrast: The mineral is *talc*; the product sold for skin is usually called *talcum powder*.

gloss: A speech or a serious conversation about a particular subject.
examples: She gave a *talk* on climate policy.
We need to have a *talk* about your grades.
There are three *talks* before lunch.

gloss: A Mexican dish of seasoned corn dough steamed in a corn husk, usually around a filling.
examples: His grandmother makes *tamales* every Christmas.
I ordered a pork *tamale* and a side of rice.
The *tamales* come wrapped in husks that you peel off.
contrast: One is a *tamale*, two are *tamales*; the husk is never eaten.

gloss: A sour-sweet tropical fruit pod used in sauces, candy, and drinks.
examples: The sauce gets its tang from *tamarind*.
She bought a block of *tamarind* paste at the Asian market.
*Tamarind* soda is sold in every corner store there.

gloss: A pair working together, or a bicycle built for two riders one behind the other.
examples: The two agencies worked in *tandem* on the rescue.
They rented a *tandem* at the beach.
The two drugs are given in *tandem*.

gloss: A line that touches a curve at one point, or a sudden change of subject.
examples: He went off on a *tangent* about his car.
The lecture kept wandering onto *tangents*.
Draw a *tangent* to the circle at point A.

gloss: A dramatic ballroom dance from Argentina, or the music written for it.
examples: They danced a slow *tango* at the reception.
The band played two *tangos* in a row.
She has been taking *tango* lessons since March.

countability: countable, and uncountable as a substance
gloss: A bitter natural substance in tea, red wine, and tree bark that dries the mouth.
examples: This wine has firm *tannins*.
Tea left to steep too long tastes of *tannin*.
*Tannins* soften as the wine ages in the bottle.

gloss: A long flat worm that lives in the intestines of a person or animal.
examples: The vet found a *tapeworm* in the cat.
Undercooked pork can carry *tapeworms*.
One dose of the medicine kills the *tapeworm*.

gloss: A starch from the cassava root, used in puddings and in the chewy pearls in bubble tea.
examples: She made *tapioca* pudding for dessert.
The drink is full of *tapioca* pearls.
*Tapioca* thickens the pie filling without clouding it.

gloss: A large sheet of waterproof cloth or plastic used as a cover.
examples: They threw a *tarpaulin* over the woodpile.
The damaged roof was patched with a blue *tarpaulin*.
Two *tarpaulins* covered the infield during the rain delay.
contrast: In everyday American speech this is almost always shortened to *tarp*.

gloss: A narrow-leaved herb with a mild licorice flavor, common in French cooking.
examples: The sauce needs fresh *tarragon*.
*Tarragon* goes well with chicken and eggs.
She grows *tarragon* in a pot on the deck.

gloss: An open pastry shell filled with fruit or cream and baked without a top crust.
examples: She brought a lemon *tart* to dinner.
The bakery sells small fruit *tarts* by the register.
This *tart* has a shortbread crust.

gloss: A child who tells adults about other children's misbehavior.
examples: Nobody likes a *tattletale*.
His little sister is a total *tattletale*.
The other kids called him a *tattletale* for a week.

gloss: A permanent design made by putting ink under the skin.
examples: He has a *tattoo* of an anchor on his forearm.
Both of her arms are covered in *tattoos*.
Getting a *tattoo* removed takes several sessions.

gloss: A grayish-brown color often used in clothing and home decorating.
examples: The walls are painted a soft *taupe*.
She chose *taupe* for the new curtains.
*Taupe* goes with almost anything.
contrast: Said TOHP, rhyming with *hope* — not TAWP and not two syllables.

gloss: A system for sorting things into named groups, especially living things.
examples: Linnaeus created the *taxonomy* we still use for species.
The team built a *taxonomy* of customer complaints.
Different *taxonomies* place the fungus in different families.

gloss: The work or profession of giving lessons.
examples: She went into *teaching* right after college.
*Teaching* pays less than she expected.
He splits his time between research and *teaching*.

gloss: A hard, oily tropical wood used for outdoor furniture and boat decks.
examples: The patio set is solid *teak*.
*Teak* holds up well in rain and sun.
The whole deck was laid in *teak*.

gloss: A covered pot with a spout and handle for boiling water on a stove.
examples: The *teakettle* started whistling.
Put the *teakettle* on, would you?
She keeps a copper *teakettle* on the back burner.
contrast: A *teakettle* boils the water on the stove; the pot you brew the tea in is a *teapot*.

gloss: A single drop of the liquid that comes from crying, or a shape like it.
examples: A *teardrop* rolled down her cheek.
The pendant is shaped like a *teardrop*.
He has a small *teardrop* tattooed under one eye.

gloss: A movie, book, or song made to bring the audience to tears.
examples: Bring tissues, because it is a real *tearjerker*.
The channel shows holiday *tearjerkers* all December.
The last chapter is a *tearjerker*.

gloss: A short advertisement or clip meant to stir up interest in something coming later.
examples: The studio released a thirty-second *teaser*.
The subject line is just a *teaser* to get you to open the email.
They posted two *teasers* before the full trailer.

gloss: Someone who is skilled at or very interested in computers and technology.
examples: Ask a *techie* to set up the router.
The neighborhood is full of young *techies*.
He is the family *techie*.

gloss: A small point of rules or law that can decide a case even though it seems unimportant.
examples: The case was thrown out on a *technicality*.
He won the argument on a *technicality*.
Let us not get lost in *technicalities*.

gloss: A style of fast electronic dance music built on repeating machine-made beats.
examples: The club plays *techno* until four in the morning.
He has been into *techno* since high school.
*Techno* came out of Detroit in the 1980s.

gloss: The study of how the huge plates of the earth's crust move and reshape the surface.
examples: Plate *tectonics* explains why earthquakes cluster along the coast.
The class spent a week on *tectonics*.
*Tectonics* raised the Himalayas over millions of years.
contrast: Though it ends in -s, *tectonics* takes a singular verb: plate tectonics explains, not explain.

gloss: Someone who never drinks alcohol.
examples: He has been a *teetotaler* since college.
The host keeps juice on hand for the *teetotalers*.
As a *teetotaler*, she always ends up driving everyone home.
contrast: American spelling has one l — *teetotaler*; British writing doubles it as *teetotaller*.

gloss: A short message that used to be sent by telegraph and delivered on paper.
examples: Her family got the *telegram* two weeks after he died.
People sent *telegrams* before long-distance calls got cheap.
The *telegram* was only eight words long.

gloss: A nineteenth-century system, or the machine used for it, that sent messages as signals over wires.
examples: News of the battle traveled by *telegraph*.
The museum has a working *telegraph* from 1870.
Early *telegraphs* could carry only one message at a time.
